column4: The section joins a wet south wind, cloud, rain, and mercy; this ayah sends winds as glad tidings before mercy, then has them carry heavy clouds, and closes by comparing rain-revived land with resurrection.
The section describes a cloud whose layers ride one another; this ayah describes God driving clouds, joining them, piling them into a mass, and rain coming from within.
The prose says wind spreads cloud in the sky; this ayah explicitly has winds stir clouds and God spread them across the sky before rain falls and people rejoice.
The source's و س م gloss pictures first rain stamping earth with vegetation; this ayah calls the reader to see the traces of God's mercy as He revives earth after death.
The section links a moist wind, cloud, rain, and green earth; this ayah sends winds that raise clouds, brings rain, and revives dead land, then compares this with resurrection.
The section's dictionary form الغيث is rain that repairs people's condition, and its ح م د link meets this ayah's الغيث, spreading of mercy, and description of God as الْحَمِيد.
The section's cloud-and-rain image is stated directly here: abundant water descends from rain clouds (الْمُعْصِرَاتِ) to produce grain and plants in the following ayat.
The section describes rain's green trace on earth; this ayah says water is poured down abundantly, and the following ayat (80:26–32) name the crops and fodder that result.
The section pictures rain writing green onto soil; this ayah says the earth is split open for growth, continuing the water-to-food sequence begun at 80:25.
The section's rain-grown vegetation is made concrete by this ayah's grain, one yield in the crop list between poured water (80:25) and provision (80:32).
The section's rain-stamped soil produces plants; this ayah adds grapes and green fodder to the yield following poured water (80:25).
The section's rain-grown earth is specified here as olives and palms, in the crop sequence following poured water (80:25).
The section describes land made green by rain; this ayah adds densely planted gardens to the sequence that begins with poured water (80:25).
The section links rain-grown plants to sustenance; this ayah names fruit and pasture, completing the yield between poured water (80:25) and provision for people and livestock (80:32).
The section links نَعْمَةُ العيش to freshness and rain-grown provision; here the different ن ع م form أَنْعَامِكُمْ names livestock receiving that provision, after the fruit and pasture of 80:31.
The section says rain improves people's condition and leaves green on earth; this ayah drives water to barren land so crops grow for people and their livestock.
The section's well scene appears directly: Moses arrives at Midian's water and finds people watering their flocks.
The section brings together water given to two women, shade, and the address رَبِّ; here Moses waters them, withdraws to the shade, and asks his Lord for whatever good He sends.
The section describes a pulley lowering a bucket into a well and Yusuf being found; here a caravan's water drawer lowers his bucket and discovers a boy.
The section treats a deep, full well as a support for life; this ayah asks who could bring flowing water if their water sank into the earth, making the well's gift reversible and dependent on God.

The section sets the straight path beside abundant water that supports the traveler; this ayah joins those details explicitly: if they remain upright on the path, God gives them abundant water (مَاءً غَدَقًا).
The section joins guidance with water that keeps a traveler going; Ibrahim's statement here says his Lord feeds and gives him drink (يَسْقِينِ), following guidance in 26:78.

The section's ر ب ب gloss says a cloud grows plants; here good land brings forth its vegetation by its Lord's permission, while the preceding ayah (7:57) supplies the wind and heavy cloud that precede this scene.
The section's cloud grows plants and rain leaves food on earth; this ayah links water sent from the sky with fruits provided for people.
The section's layered cloud and rain image is echoed by this ayah's clouds held between heaven and earth, rain sent down, and earth revived with it.
The section says rain-grown green is the mark left on soil; this ayah shows water from the sky bringing out varied crops, grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates.
The section names the wet south wind before rain; this ayah sends winds that fertilize, then sends down water from the sky.
The section's س م و dictionary note says Arabs call cloud and rain "sky"; this ayah uses مِنَ السَّمَاءِ for the source of water that people drink and vegetation grows from.
The section's rain leaves a green, useful mark; this ayah names grain, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits grown by that water, continuing 16:10.
The section describes rain as benefit that renews the land; this ayah says God sends water from the sky and revives earth after its death.
The section joins a road with rain-grown plants; this ayah says God made paths through the earth, sent water from the sky, and brought forth varied plants.
The section's source gloss includes pasture and enduring plants; this ayah tells people to eat and pasture their livestock, after 20:53 describes the water and paired plants.
The section's rain leaves growth on soil; this ayah describes lifeless earth swelling and producing lovely plants when water descends, as a sign of resurrection.
The section pictures rain writing green onto earth; this ayah asks whether God sending water makes the land turn green.
The section describes abundant water gathered in a well; this ayah says water is sent down in measure and lodged in the earth, while also stressing that God can take it away.
The section links gathered water to green growth and provision; this ayah names gardens, date palms, and grapes that follow the measured water in 23:18.
The section joins wind, cloud, rain, and mercy; this ayah sends winds before mercy and sends pure water down from the sky.
The section treats water as what sustains life and people's affairs; this ayah says the rain revives dead land and supplies drink for people and livestock, completing 25:48.
The section's rain grows the earth's plants; this ayah asks who sends water from the sky and grows gardens whose trees people could not have grown themselves.
The section presents rain as restoring people's condition; this ayah says God sends water from the sky and revives earth after its death.
The section links rain and renewed life; this ayah joins lightning, hope and fear, rain from the sky, and the revival of dead earth.
The section quotes rain sent after people have despaired (42:28); this neighboring ayah says they had despaired before rain came, completing the cloud-and-rain passage of 30:48–50.
The section's growing cloud brings plants from earth; this ayah says God sends rain and grows every kind of noble plant.
The section's rain leaves green growth as a mark on land; this ayah presents dead earth revived and grain brought forth for people to eat.
The section describes rain's green trace on soil; this ayah says barren land stirs and grows after water falls on it.
The section's cloud provides life-giving water; this ayah says rain descends in measure and revives a dead country.
The section links rain to a green mark on earth; this ayah names blessed rain, grain, and growing gardens.
The section's rain produces lasting plant growth; this ayah specifies tall date palms with clustered fruit, continuing the provision in 50:9.
The section links rain-grown plants to provision; this ayah says the crops and fruit are provision for servants and that dead land is revived, completing 50:9–10.
The section describes plants growing out of earth; this ayah uses that image for human creation, saying God grew people from the earth like plants.
The section's rain-cloud produces vegetation; this ayah names grain and plants from the rain in 78:14.
The section asks the reader to see how rain becomes provision; this ayah tells people to look at their food, and the next ayat (80:25–32) trace it to water, crops, and pasture.
The section includes Moses at water, helping people water their flocks; this ayah has Moses strike a rock and twelve springs gush out for his people to drink.
The section presents water from the sky and water drawn from earth as sources of life; in Noah's flood this ayah reverses them, ordering the earth to swallow its water and the sky to cease.
The section names the plan to cast Yusuf into the well's hidden depth; this ayah voices that plan, and 12:15 narrates its execution.
The section's Yusuf image is a boy in a well; this ayah recounts his brothers putting him in the well and the revelation he receives there, following their plan in 12:10.
The section links rain and water to sustenance; this ayah says God sends water, brings out fruits as provision, and makes rivers available.
The section's ن ع م gloss describes the freshness and goodness of life; this ayah calls God's provisions نعمة and says they cannot be counted, following the water and fruit in 14:32–33.
The section joins a straight path with water supporting a traveler; this ayah places rivers and paths together as signs by which people find their way.
The section depends on a full well and water that can be drawn; this ayah warns that the garden's water could sink into the earth beyond reach.
The source section gives رَبَب a secondary dictionary sense of sweet water; this ayah calls one of the two meeting waters عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and contrasts it with salt and bitter water.
The section says Ibrahim describes the Lord of the worlds while joining guidance to drinking; this ayah names the Lord of the worlds, and 26:78–79 specify guidance, food, and drink.
The section sets the straight path beside the traveler's water; Ibrahim says his Lord guides him here, immediately before saying that He feeds and gives drink in 26:79.
The section connects a journey, a request for guidance, and the well at Midian; this ayah has Moses set out toward Midian and ask his Lord to guide him, before he reaches its water in 28:23.

The section calls water the support that keeps an affair standing and sustains the traveler; this ayah uses قِيَامًا for property as people's means of support, a specific parallel in the function of a life-sustaining resource.
The section names deep, plentiful well-water as what sustains a traveler; this ayah asks people to consider the water they drink.
The section's dictionary note calls gathered water sweet and also describes sky-borne rain; this ayah asks whether people send down their drinking water from the clouds or God does.
The section names a tender plant that does not wither in summer; this ayah's rain-grown vegetation flourishes, then is harvested and vanishes, making persistence the boundary.

The section describes abundant gathered water and green growth that remains; this ayah's torrent carries foam that disappears while what benefits people stays, a parallel about water's lasting yield rather than the same well scene.
The section's رب root gloss includes a plant that does not wither in summer; this ayah's rain-grown vegetation turns dry and scattered, making the seasonal contrast explicit.
The section names a green plant that does not wither in summer; this ayah shows rain-grown crops turning yellow and then to debris, specifying the limit of that persistence.
The section describes life-giving rain arriving from the sky; Noah's flood reverses that provision into overwhelming water from above, and 54:12 adds earth's springs meeting it.
The section pairs rain from above with water drawn from earth; this flood scene opens earth into springs and makes the two sources meet, while 54:11 supplies the sky's torrent.
The section's secondary dictionary gloss calls water sweet; this ayah says God could make drinking water bitter instead, reversing that gift after the question in 56:68–69.
The section invokes a plant that remains green through summer; this ayah compares worldly life to vegetation that grows, yellows, and crumbles, making the opposite course of the crop explicit.
The section describes a tender plant that does not wither in summer; this ayah names pasture brought forth from earth, and 87:5 shows it turning to dark stubble.
The section's رب root gloss preserves green growth through summer; this ayah turns pasture into dark stubble, the direct contrary endpoint to that persistence after the pasture appears in 87:4.

This rainstorm's darkness, thunder, and lightning presents the cloud's frightening face; it contrasts with the section's cloud as rain-bearing growth and mercy, though the storm here serves as a simile.
The section links rain to growth on earth; this ayah compares good giving to a garden on high ground that yields twice when heavy rain falls, with even light rain sufficient.
The section joins cloud, water, and provision in Moses' journey; this ayah gives Moses' people shade from cloud and twelve springs for drinking, each with a known drinking place.
The section connects ground, water, and plant growth; this ayah places rivers and paired fruits in the spread earth, a concrete landscape where water and yield meet.
The section describes layered, heavy cloud; this ayah shows lightning and raises heavy clouds, with fear and hope accompanying the weather.

The section's ن ع م dictionary gloss describes life's freshness and goodness; this ayah says God's نعمة cannot be counted, following the rain, crops, rivers, and other provisions described in 16:10–17.
The section links water drawn from earth to useful growth; this ayah describes a garden of grapes and palms with crops between them, in the paired garden scene continued at 18:33.
The section brings water together with plant yield; this ayah says both gardens produce fruit and have a river running through them, continuing the garden scene of 18:32.
The section treats water as what sustains people and livestock; this ayah makes the link more basic by saying God created every moving creature from water.
The source section gives رَبَب a secondary dictionary sense of sweet water; this ayah names one sea as fresh and sweet and contrasts it with salty, bitter water.
The section joins rain to soil's growth; this ayah sends water from the sky and brings out fruits of varied colors.
The section describes earth made productive by water; this ayah says God made gardens of palms and grapes and caused springs to gush within them, following dead land revived in 36:33.
The section links growth and gathered water to provision; this ayah says people eat the fruit of the gardens and notes that they did not make it themselves, completing 36:34.
The section's cloud and rain renew the land; this ayah names the alternation of night and day, provision from the sky, winds, and the revival of dead earth as signs.
The section pictures rain leaving green growth on soil; this ayah asks people to consider what they sow, immediately before asking who makes it grow in 56:64.
The section says a rain-bearing cloud grows plants; this ayah asks whether people make their crops grow or God does, continuing the sowing question in 56:63.
The section names a tender plant that does not wither in summer; this ayah says God could make the crop dry into fragments, the reversal of enduring green growth.

The section's و س م dictionary entry describes the first rain stamping earth with vegetation; this ayah uses the same source root in سَنَسِمُهُ for a punitive mark on a person's snout, reversing the earth's beneficial green mark.
The section describes a well as a source of drinkable water; this ayah describes a spring from which God's servants drink and which they cause to flow.
The source section's secondary رَبَب gloss calls water sweet; this ayah names fresh, sweet water given to drink, alongside the earth's firm mountains.
The section's rain grows useful plants; this ayah adds thick gardens to the grain and plants in 78:15, all following water poured from clouds in 78:14.
The section says water comes from earth through a well and supports growth; this ayah explicitly says God brought out the earth's water and its pasture.
The section's rain and well water serve people and animals; this ayah calls the pasture and other provisions enjoyment for people and their livestock, completing 79:31–32.
If the sky's "return" here evokes recurring rain, it pairs with the earth's fissure in 86:12, recalling the section's rain-to-soil growth; that reading is an echo, not an explicit well scene.
The section says rain leaves growth on earth; this ayah swears by the earth's fissure, paired with the sky's return in 86:11.
